cards.prompt: Import pandas using its standard alias.
cards.why: Every pandas tutorial, doc page, and codebase uses the pd alias — it's a universal convention, not just a shortcut.
cards.whenToUse: The first line of any script or notebook that touches pandas.
cards.commonMistake: Importing as a different alias — it works, but makes your code harder for others (and Stack Overflow answers) to follow.
cards.example: # no output — makes pd.DataFrame, pd.Series, etc. available

cards.prompt: Create a Series — a single labeled column of data — from a list of numbers.
cards.why: A Series is pandas' 1D building block: values plus an index. A DataFrame is just a collection of Series sharing one index.
cards.whenToUse: Representing a single sequence of values that needs labels, not just a plain Python list.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting a Series to print like a list — it always shows its index alongside each value.

cards.prompt: Create a DataFrame from a dict of equal-length lists, one list per column.
cards.why: Each dict key becomes a column name, and each list becomes that column's values — the most common way to build a small DataFrame by hand.
cards.whenToUse: Constructing sample data, or assembling results you've computed in plain Python into a table.
cards.commonMistake: Passing lists of different lengths — pandas raises a ValueError instead of padding the shorter one.

cards.prompt: Check how many rows and columns df has.
cards.why: shape returns a (rows, columns) tuple in one call — the fastest way to sanity-check a DataFrame's size.
cards.whenToUse: Right after loading or filtering data, to confirm you got what you expected.
cards.commonMistake: Calling it like a method (df.shape()) — shape is an attribute, not a method, so it has no parentheses.

cards.prompt: Preview the first 3 rows of df.
cards.why: head() is the fastest way to eyeball a DataFrame's shape and column contents without printing the whole thing.
cards.whenToUse: Right after loading data, or after any transformation, to spot-check the result.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting head() defaults to 5 rows when called with no argument, not 10.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9
# 2   West     Bags       80      8

cards.prompt: Preview the last 2 rows of df.
cards.why: tail() mirrors head() for the end of the DataFrame — useful for checking that a sort or append landed correctly.
cards.whenToUse: Confirming the end of a DataFrame after sorting, appending, or a time-ordered load.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming tail() reverses row order — it doesn't, it just shows the last n rows in their existing order.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 6  North    Shoes       50      5
# 7  North     Bags       65      6

cards.prompt: Print a summary of df's columns, dtypes, and non-null counts.
cards.why: info() is the single fastest way to spot missing values and wrong dtypes (like numbers stored as text) in one glance.
cards.whenToUse: Right after loading unfamiliar data, before you trust any column's contents.
cards.commonMistake: Confusing info() with describe() — info() is about structure (dtypes, nulls), describe() is about numeric statistics.
cards.example:
# RangeIndex: 8 entries, 0 to 7
# region, category, revenue, units — 8 non-null each

cards.prompt: Get summary statistics (count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max) for df's numeric columns.
cards.why: describe() gives you a quick statistical fingerprint of every numeric column — a fast way to spot outliers or skew.
cards.whenToUse: Getting an at-a-glance feel for a numeric column's distribution.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting describe() silently skips non-numeric columns by default (unless you pass include='all').

cards.prompt: Check the data type of every column in df.
cards.why: dtypes reveals when numbers were loaded as text (object) — a frequent cause of silently-wrong math and comparisons.
cards.whenToUse: Right after loading data, especially from CSV, before doing any arithmetic on a column.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming a column that looks numeric is actually numeric — CSV loads default text-looking numbers to object if anything in the column doesn't parse cleanly.
cards.example:
# region       object
# category     object
# revenue       int64
# units         int64
# dtype: object

cards.prompt: Get the column names of df.
cards.why: columns returns an Index of labels — useful for checking exact spelling/casing before referencing a column elsewhere.
cards.whenToUse: Confirming what a column is actually called before selecting or renaming it.
cards.commonMistake: Treating df.columns like a plain list — it's an Index object, though most list operations (list(df.columns)) still work on it.

cards.prompt: Get df's row index (its row labels).
cards.why: Every DataFrame has a row index, even if you never set one — by default it's a simple 0..n RangeIndex.
cards.whenToUse: Checking whether a DataFrame has a meaningful custom index (like dates) or just the default integer one.
cards.commonMistake: Confusing the index with a regular column — it's a separate axis, not one of df.columns.

cards.prompt: Count how many rows df has using a plain Python built-in, not a pandas-specific method. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: len() on a DataFrame counts its rows, same as it would count items in a list — one of the few plain-Python builtins that works directly on pandas objects.
cards.whenToUse: A quick row count when you don't need the column count too (unlike shape).
cards.commonMistake: Expecting len(df) to count columns — it always counts rows, matching len() on the row index.

cards.prompt: Check whether df has zero rows.
cards.why: empty is a quick boolean check — useful after a filter that might return nothing, before you try to use the result.
cards.whenToUse: Guarding code that would error or behave oddly on a zero-row DataFrame, e.g. after a filter with no matches.
cards.commonMistake: Calling it as a method (df.empty()) — like shape, it's an attribute, not a method.

cards.prompt: Which of these creates a pandas Series, not a DataFrame?
cards.why: Series is the 1D constructor; DataFrame is 2D even when built from a single-key dict or a single-column list of lists.
cards.whenToUse: Deciding which constructor to reach for based on whether you need one labeled column or a full table.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2, 3]}) returns a Series because it only has one column — it's still a DataFrame.
